summary:
Berlin is a Land of the Federal Republic of Germany. Federal constitutional and equality protections apply in every Land, national identity documents and marriage law are uniform, and no Land can remove that federal floor. Legal gender recognition is therefore governed nationally, not by the Berlin Senate.

The Self-Determination Act, passed in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251 and in force from 1 November 2024, replaced the 1980 Transsexuals Act, whose surgery and sterilisation requirements the Federal Constitutional Court struck down in January 2011. Transgender, intersex and non-binary adults can change their legal gender by self-determination with three months' notice. A 'divers' marker has been available on birth certificates, passports and driving licences since 1 January 2019 under the Third Gender Act, but it requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status, and it was clarified in April 2019 as applying to intersex people only.

Custody is the sharpest documented exposure. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and reports that placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; it runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several Länder have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage.

Berlin's own prison service states that legislation has created a basis for considering trans, inter* and non-binary people held in custody, that its staff are responsible for taking each detainee's individual needs into account within the legal framework, and it sets out gender-segregated placement, intake procedures and counselling and support offers across the city's facilities, including JVA Moabit and JVA für Frauen Berlin. How the exception is applied in practice is unsettled, and outcomes have gone both ways. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle said Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry had been changed to female at the end of 2024, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia, DW reported on 16 July 2026 that she had been transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman, with authorities citing the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. In the Penelope Frank case, covered by DW in August 2023, a climate activist with a legal male registration faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted, and the reporting described German prisons as offering few safe spaces for trans inmates.

Recorded anti-LGBTI violence in Berlin is high by national standards. MANEO, the city's anti-violence documentation project, logged 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents in Berlin in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, drawn from 1,014 new reports — a new high for reporting volume. Its 12 May 2026 release lists insults, threats and physical attacks on public transport, in parks and in streets, with Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten the most affected districts, plus 58 attacks on LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO states the figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, and reports that its own counselling centre was attacked several times in 2025.

At the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day, MANEO reports that a vehicle drove into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman, injuring several people and forcing the event to be cancelled. The project offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line on 030-2163336, staffed daily 17:00 to 19:00.

Nationally the picture is one of rising pressure on Pride events. The amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events across Germany in 2024 and 30 so far in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including an attack with boiling water, and runs a €100,000 CSD support fund focused on eastern Germany. Maneo, the Berlin anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades such as Berlin and Cologne were not specifically threatened and that smaller towns are hardest to police. Berlin CSD organisers have publicly urged vigilance with hundreds of thousands of attendees expected. A queer café owner in Berlin-Neukölln reported 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.

Airport screening has produced a specific documented complaint. The DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024. According to her account, reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity in what she called a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment; she provided the publication a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected spaces has been contested in the leisure sector since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a public debate about registered trans women's access, and reporting from Berlin on how saunas and similar venues handle trans women followed months of argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office found that a July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed by the Education Minister in her own ministry contradicted constitutional equality protection. Since May 2020 a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has carried penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025. In June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes, including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.
tangentialFactors:
Berlin's recorded incident volume sits above what the national Pride figures suggest for a single city: 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents were documented in Berlin in 2025 against 30 right-wing-extremist attacks on Pride events recorded nationwide in the same year to date. The two counts measure different things, and neither is comparable to the other as a crime rate.

The Liebich and Frank cases show the custody question turning on facts specific to each prisoner rather than on the wording of the statute, and both were reported by a national broadcaster rather than resolved by a court ruling published in the sources. Placement in Berlin facilities is described by the Berlin prison service in terms of individual assessment, which does not by itself indicate which outcome a given detainee should expect.

The Rhineland-Palatinate prison act amendment and the Lower Saxony provision cited by the Criminological Research Institute are other Länder's statutes. They show the direction of travel across the federation but do not bind a Berlin facility.

The leisure-sector argument concerns the period immediately after the Self-Determination Act came into force, and the sources document the guideline and the debate rather than any binding rule for Berlin venues.
localsOnly:
Residents change their legal gender marker through the self-determination procedure with three months' notice to the registry office; no medical diagnosis, surgery or sterilisation is required, and the route is available to transgender, intersex and non-binary adults. The 'divers' marker remains conditional on a doctor's statement confirming intersex status.

The Berlin prison service maintains a dedicated information page for trans, inter* and non-binary people in custody, setting out placement rules, intake procedures and the counselling and support contacts available across the city's facilities, including JVA Moabit and JVA für Frauen Berlin.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in health services and education is prohibited under the General Act on Equal Treatment. The conversion therapy ban applies to minors nationwide, with up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring.

The Federal Anti-Discrimination Office has assessed the July 2025 ban on gender-inclusive language imposed within the federal education ministry as contradicting constitutional equality protection.

Victim support runs through MANEO, which provides counselling and an anonymous reporting line on 030-2163336, staffed daily 17:00 to 19:00, and through the national STOP the HATE campaign, which maintains a counselling finder sorted by topic, an LSBTIQ* crisis line and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state the outcome of BASHKKA's complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment. The complaint is documented; any decision, settlement or finding is unresolved here.

Whether Berlin has amended its own prison statute to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, in the way Rhineland-Palatinate amended its act with effect from 1 March 2026, is not sourced. The Berlin prison service page describes existing practice and legal basis only.

Whether the vehicle that struck the crowd at the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day was directed at the event as an anti-LGBTI act is unresolved in the sources; MANEO's account reports the vehicle, the death and the cancellation without establishing motive.

MANEO states that its 2025 figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, so the recorded totals understate incidents. The share of those incidents that were specifically anti-trans as distinct from broader LSBTIQ+-hostile is not broken down in the sources.

The full text and application of the new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act were not reviewed for this record; only its 1 March 2026 entry into force is sourced.
